Abstract— We introduce R2LDM, an innovative approach for
generating dense and accurate 4D radar point clouds, guided by
corresponding LiDAR point clouds. Instead of utilizing range
images or bird’s eye view (BEV) images, we represent both
LiDAR and 4D radar point clouds using voxel features, which
more effectively capture 3D shape information. Subsequently,
we propose the Latent Voxel Diffusion Model (LVDM), which
performs the diffusion process in the latent space. Additionally,
a novel Latent Point Cloud Reconstruction (LPCR) module
is utilized to reconstruct point clouds from high-dimensional
latent voxel features. As a result, R2LDM effectively generates
LiDAR-like point clouds from paired raw radar data. We
evaluate our approach on two different datasets, and the
experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves 6to
10-fold densification of radar point clouds, outperforming stateof-the-art baselines in 4D radar point cloud super-resolution.
Furthermore, the enhanced radar point clouds generated by
our method significantly improve downstream tasks, achieving
up to 31.7% improvement in point cloud registration recall rate
and 24.9% improvement in object detection accuracy.
I. INTRODUCTION
4D millimeter-wave radar [1], [2], [3] has emerged as a
critical sensor in autonomous driving, attracting significant
attention from both academia and industry for its ability
to provide 3D point cloud data and instantaneous velocity
measurements. Additionally, the longer wavelength of 4D
radar makes it nearly immune to interference from small
particles in fog and rain, allowing it to operate reliably under
challenging weather conditions. Compared to LiDAR and

Despite these advantages, the point clouds provided by
4D Radar are two orders of magnitude lower than those
from LiDAR [4], resulting in not only sparse data but also
a lack of context information [5]. In addition, multipath
effects introduce artifacts, ghost points, and false targets into
radar point clouds, making them susceptible to inaccuracies.
Evidently, these factors significantly hinder the application of
4D radar in autonomous driving. This motivates us to seek an
approach that effectively mitigates noise and sparsity of radar
point clouds, enabling robust, continuous, and reliable allweather sensing for downstream autonomous driving tasks.
It is noteworthy that recently, generative model approaches
have achieved significant success in LiDAR point cloud
upsampling and completion tasks, with diffusion models
demonstrating the most outstanding performance. Given the
powerful generative capabilities of diffusion models and
their suitability for high-noise scenarios [6], it is intuitive
to consider adapting diffusion models to the task of radar
point cloud super-resolution, using LiDAR as ground-truth
supervision [7], [8] . However, directly applying diffusion to
point clouds is challenging. Existing methods encode dense
LiDAR data into a range image [9] before the diffusion
process. Given the fundamental differences in the point cloud
generation principles of 4D radar and LiDAR, range image
encoding is not well-suited for 4D radar point clouds, posing
significant difficulties for this task.
To address these challenges, we propose a novel 4D radar
super-resolution framework, R2LDM, which enhances sparse
4D radar points into dense, LiDAR-like points. Specifically,
to develop a unified representation of both radar and LiDAR
point clouds, we introduce the Latent Voxel Diffusion Model
(LVDM), which encodes 4D radar and LiDAR point clouds
as latent voxel features, performing the diffusion process
in the latent space. We demonstrate that this approach

In contrast to similar work [10], our diffusion model captures the distribution of point clouds at a high-dimensional
feature level, thus requiring an additional module to reconstruct the point cloud back into real 3D space. Inspired by
[11], we propose a novel Latent Point Cloud Reconstruction (LPCR) module, which employs sparse convolution to
predict an occupancy probability mask and offset for each
voxel from latent features. Experimental results demonstrate
that this approach robustly predicts voxel points closely
approximating the ground truth.
To alleviate the training challenges caused by the large
difference in point cloud density between the two modalities
(e.g., the presence of more empty voxels in Radar data), we
divide the training process into two stages. In the first stage,
we train the LPCR module to enable the model to reconstruct
3D point clouds from sparse features in the latent space, and
in the second stage, we train the LVDM module to learn
the feature distribution from 4D Radar to LiDAR. We conducted experiments on both public and self-made datasets,
demonstrating that R2LDM outperforms all baseline methods
in the point cloud super-resolution task. Additionally, we
validated the effectiveness of the generated point cloud in
downstream tasks such as point cloud registration. Overall,
the contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
• We propose a novel 4D mmWave radar point clouds
super-resolution method that generates dense and accurate LiDAR-like point clouds. To the best of our
knowledge, this is the first approach to model the
transformation from 4D Radar to LiDAR utilizing a
latent space diffusion process.
• We propose an innovative Latent Point Cloud Reconstruction (LPCR) module that directly reconstructs point
clouds from latent features. This approach ensures robust voxel-wise predictions and achieves reconstruction
results that closely match the ground truth.
• We validate our framework on two different datasets,
demonstrating that our method outperforms state-ofthe-art baselines, achieving up to 31.7% improvement
in point cloud registration recall rate and 24.9% improvement in object detection accuracy compared to the
original radar point cloud.

clouds [14], [15], learning-based point cloud densification
methods exhibit superior potential. Chamseddine [16] employs PointNet [17] to differentiate between ghost and real
targets, leading to precise radar point cloud generation.
Prabhakara [8] introduces RadarHD, which utilizes a UNet [18] to transform low-resolution radar point clouds
into dense LiDAR-like point clouds. Zhang [4] proposed a
single-chip mmWave radar point cloud construction method
designed for autonomous navigation of MAVs. However,
the aforementioned works are primarily based on 2D data.
In contrast, our R2LDM enables effective 3D point cloud
densification while preserving the scene context.
Difffusion Models Recently, generative models [19], [20],
[21], [22] have garnered widespread attention and found
broad applications. Among these, diffusion models [23] have
achieved significant success in the field of image generation
with notable advancements such as LDMs [24]. Researchers
have also developed language-guided diffusion models [25],
[26] and other controllable diffusion models [27], which
demonstrate the immense potential of diffusion models. Our
R2LDM is also a conditional diffusion model, capable of
taking sparse millimeter-wave radar point clouds as conditional inputs and generating dense LiDAR-like point clouds
as output.

promising approach for synthesizing realistic LiDAR point

facilitate LiDAR synthesis. The pioneering work by Caccia
[28] explore the application of generative models to LiDAR
scenes, proposing LiDARVAE and LiDARGAN for unconditional generation and noisy LiDAR reconstruction. R2DM
[9] presented a novel generative model for LiDAR data that
can generate diverse and high-fidelity 3D scene point clouds
based on the image representation of range and reflectance

Luan [6] introduces a mean-reverting SDE-based diffusion
model for 4D mmWave radar point cloud super-resolution.
However, this approach converts radar point clouds into BEV
images, where the height is encoded in the channel. This
scheme leads to each pixel representing at most one point,
resulting in sparse point clouds and limiting performance.

voxel features, performs the diffusion process in the latent
space, and effectively densifies the radar point cloud through
the LPCR module, significantly enhancing the point cloud

III. PROPOSED METHOD
This section expounds on the details of the R2LDM. In
Sec. III-A, we discuss our design choice of latent voxel
features for data representation. In Sec. III-B, we formulate
the task of enhanced radar point clouds generation with
R2LDM. In Sec. III-C, we define the latent voxel diffusion
model with 4D radar as the condition. In Sec. III-D, we
present how the latent point clouds reconstruction module
work. In Sec. III-E, we define the training objectives in two
stages. Fig. 3 illustrates the overall R2LDM framework.
A. Data Representation
Effective representation of point cloud data is crucial for
radar-to-LiDAR super-resolution. Existing methods, such as
range image and BEV image encoding, struggle to adapt
to both radar and LiDAR point clouds due to their distinct
generation processes. As shown in Fig. 4, these differences
hinder the use of traditional encoding methods for both
point cloud types. To address this, we adopt a voxel feature
encoder, which better captures point cloud data and preserves
high-dimensional latent features, facilitating the diffusion
process. More details on data processing are in Sec. IV-B.
B. Problem Formulation
The input point clouds and our generated point clouds are
denoted as P and ˆP, respectively, where P, ˆP ∈RN×3. As
described in Sec. III-A , we use the Voxel Feature Encoder
E to encode P into latent feature F = E(P), where F ∈
Rh×w×d. Our Latent Point Cloud Reconstruction module
serves as a decoder D to reconstruct ˆP = D(F) = D(E(P)).
For the diffusion process, we formulate the point cloud voxel

C. Latent Voxel Diffusion Model
Directly recovering a densified point cloud feature from
pure noise is non-trivial. Therefore, we condition the process
on radar features F R and approximate the distribution of
the high-dimensional features F R and F L in the latent
space, thereby controlling the diffusion generation process.
Forward diffusion process While training, the forward
diffusion process gradually adds Gaussian noise into the
ground truth LiDAR latent feature f0 for T timesteps via
a Markov chain:

Inverse diffusion process Starting from the noisy
feature fT, the model applies the learned reverse process
mθ for T steps to obtain f0. Once f0 is reconstructed,
the corresponding point cloud is generated through the
LPCR module.
D. Latent Point Cloud Reconstruction Module
The Latent Point Cloud Reconstruction (LPCR) module is
designed to reconstruct 3D point clouds from latent features.
As shown in Fig. 4, the module employs sparse convolution
to predict an occupancy probability mask and an offset for
each voxel from the latent features. The key is that the
module operates in the latent space, which allows for efficient
and effective voxel-wise predictions.
E. Training Objectives
We divide the training into two stages. In Stage 1, we
train the Voxel Feature Encoder E and the LPCR module
to reconstruct 3D point clouds from the latent features
generated from LiDAR point clouds. In Stage 2, we train
the LVDM module to learn the mapping from the features of
both LiDAR and 4D radar point clouds as input, learning to
approximate the distribution of the high-dimensional features
in the latent space. During the inference phase, the model
takes Gaussian noise and raw radar point clouds as input
and accurately generates dense LiDAR-like point clouds, resulting
in up to 10 times densification.

IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
A. Datasets
We evaluate our framework on two datasets: the public
 datasets, e.g., KITTI [26], and self-made datasets. The
public datasets are widely used and provide a good test
ground for our framework. The self-made datasets are
custom-tailored for our specific task, ensuring the framework
performs well in real-world scenarios. Detailed descriptions
are in Sec. IV-B.
B. Model Configuration
We describe the model configuration in detail. The VFE
module uses a series of sparse convolutions with size
64×64×64, the LVDM has 5 layers, and the LPCR
module uses 3 layers of sparse convolutions. The training
parameters include the number of epochs, learning rate, etc.
We also provide specific details about the hyperparameters
in Sec. IV-C.
C. Performance Metrics
We evaluate our framework using metrics such as
F1 score, precision, recall, and F1 score for object detection.
Additionally, we compare our method with baseline methods
in terms of these metrics.

We also provide specific details about the hyperparameters

C. Performance Metrics
We evaluate our framework using metrics such as
F1 score, precision, recall, and F1 score for object detection.
Additionally, we compare our method with baseline methods

Our framework achieves an average F1 score of 31.7%
